title: This Tiny Chip Steers Light Faster Than a Blink
summary:
Blink. In the time it takes you to blink, this new chip could steer a beam of light billions of times.

Scientists at Caltech have built a device that uses one beam of light to redirect another beam in just 74 femtoseconds. A femtosecond is a quadrillionth of a second — that's a 1 followed by 15 zeros. How fast is 74 of them? About the time light needs to travel across the width of a single human hair. Whoa.

Why is this hard? Light usually doesn't like to interact with stuff. It mostly just passes through. Most devices that steer light work by pushing electrons (tiny charged particles) into higher energy states, then waiting for them to relax. That waiting creates a speed limit — usually trillionths of a second.

The Caltech team skipped the waiting. They used a strong "pump" beam of light to briefly change how a material bends light. Then a weaker "probe" beam passed through and got redirected. The change appears and vanishes almost as fast as the light pulse itself.

To make the effect stronger, they built a surface covered in tiny silicon pillars, each smaller than the wavelength of the light. These pillars trap light a little longer, so it interacts more.

Result: they steered light by angles up to 13 degrees in 74 femtoseconds. And the speed limit isn't the material — it's the laser pulses. Faster lasers could mean even faster steering.

Why care? Faster light control could mean quicker internet, more powerful computers, and super-sensitive sensors. Not bad for a chip you can't even see.
why_it_matters: The internet and computers you use every day run on light and electricity, so learning to steer light billions of times faster could one day mean quicker videos, faster downloads and gadgets we haven't invented yet.

background_read: Caltech (the California Institute of Technology, a science university in California) is where this chip was made — its researchers study light, materials and computers.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe; nothing can travel faster, which is why scientists want to use light instead of electricity inside computers and the internet.
Today, computers and the internet mostly send information as electricity through wires, but light could carry far more information — if scientists can switch and steer it fast enough.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists at Caltech.
WHAT: They built a tiny chip that uses one beam of light to steer another beam in only 74 femtoseconds.
WHERE: At Caltech, on a surface covered in tiny silicon pillars smaller than the light's wavelength.
WHY: Skipping the slow wait for electrons means light can be controlled much faster, which could lead to quicker internet, more powerful computers and super-sensitive sensors.

perspectives.description: The team steered light in 74 femtoseconds, much faster than the usual trillionths of a second, and the effect worked at angles up to 13 degrees.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: it's still a lab result
perspectives.description: This is an experiment, not a product — other scientists will need to test it and build on it before anything real uses it.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: lasers are the next limit
perspectives.description: The article says the speed limit is now the laser pulses, not the material, so even faster steering depends on building better lasers — and real devices are still years away.
